Q: Enable-BitLocker command throws error: Value does not fall within the expected range A:

I solved the problem by adding a RecoveryPasswordProtector first and then calling the Enable-BitLocker command. There was no error indication of this from Powershell but there was from cmd by invoking manage-bde -on C:

    Add-BitLockerKeyProtector -MountPoint $mountPoint -RecoveryPasswordProtector
    Enable-BitLocker -MountPoint $mountPoint -EncryptionMethod XtsAes128 -Pin $SecurePIN -TpmAndPinProtector -UsedSpaceOnly

Q: Pygame platformer: player sticks to the side of stacked tiles during collision A:

I think the problem is that as you're looping through all the tiles, the first check is for "Vertical collisions". I think that's the thing that is setting the player.vel_y to 0, causing them to "stick".

To fix that, you need to check to see if the user is next to or under the tile. So compare the x "left" and x "right" of the player and the tile to see if you need to even check for the vertical collision.

Q: Why does the `java.util.UUID` class seem to repeat its validation when parsing an input string? A:

UPDATE: See below: The first snippet is 10x faster, that's why.

Leading zeroes omitted

The first one parses the incoming UUID based solely on the position of characters: Each nibble is extracted by way of position and then bit-shifted into place. It can only work if the UUID is exactingly specified - precisely 36 characters with the dashes in exactly the expected location.

If there is any difference (either the input isn't precisely 36 characters long, or even one of the positions that ought to be a dash isn't a dash), then the first one cannot work, so it relegates to the second one.

The second one doesn't do that: It scans for the location of the dashes, then parses all data in between the dashes into longs (via parseLong) and bitshifts + bit-ors them into place.

The second one is seemingly superior; it can deal with slightly wonkily stated UUIDs. One somewhat common 'mis-formatting' of UUIDs is to omit leading zeroes.

Example:

Valid UUID : 9c5b94b1-35ad-49bb-b118-0e8fc24abf80
Weird way  : 9c5b94b1-35ad-49bb-b118-e8fc24abf80

As per RFC9562, that second form isn't 'legal'. However, there's Postel's Law to consider: Be lenient in what you accept, and strict in what you create. Postel isn't something that should be casually discarded. Failure to heed it results in things like vaunted XHTML plans to die by the wayside (XHTML is probably the most famous violation of Postel's Law and it has utterly failed, against all expectations and to the great lament of many a nerd not familiar with Postel).

Hence, while one could certainly argue against it, it's plausible that the OpenJDK team intentionally wanted to accept clear enough UUIDs even if technically they don't conform to RFC9562.

So why does the first version exist in the first place, if the second can do everything the first can, and more?

Presumably performance. I haven't put in the effort to write a JMH for it, but, applying some common sense (a very dangerous practice, reasoning about performance, I hope you permit me the transgression): parseLong is considerably more complicated than parse4Nibbles.

The base method is written to work solely on strict UUIDs (given that they are, likely, 99% of all inputs), but with the restriction that it must be as fast as possible, and that subroutine is written to accept all UUIDs that OpenJDK feels should be accepted, but gets to skate on the performance requirement. Not a bad setup.

ADDENDUM: JMH performance benchmark results

I was curious so I decided to toss these 2 versions through JMH on Java25, see if there really is a performance difference. On ARM chip:

testDashScan    thrpt   25   19718076,292 ±  425549,914  ops/s
testPositional  thrpt   25  166515283,275 ± 4535910,205  ops/s

Oof. The dash scan (fromString1) is almsot 10x slower.

JMH code:

 @Benchmark
  public Object testPositional() {
    return positional("7f1943d2-f582-11f0-8de9-0242ac120002");
  }
  
  @Benchmark
  public Object testDashScan() {
    return dashScan("7f1943d2-f582-11f0-8de9-0242ac120002");
  }

With 'positional()' being a copy/paste of fromString, except with the return fromString1 replaced with a throw statement just in case (it's never triggered, of course), and dashScan is fromString1.

Q: Nested preprocessor macro compilation problem A:

Best you can do is:

#define Curl_dyn_addn_fixed(...) Curl_dyn_addn(__VA_ARGS__)

And then use this macro instead. An extra level of nesting causes it to expand STRCONST(".") before splitting the arguments.

If you could modify the original macro, you could replace it with:

#define Curl_dyn_addn(...) curlx_dyn_addn(__VA_ARGS__)

For the same effect.

Perhaps Curl could even accept this as a PR.

Q: Can you execute commands using docker hardened images? A:

That's entirely intentional (emphasis mine):

Docker Hardened Images prioritize security through minimalism:

  • Reduced attack surface: Fewer binaries mean fewer potential vulnerabilities
  • Immutable infrastructure: Runtime containers shouldn't be modified after deployment
  • Compliance ready: Meets strict security requirements for regulated environments

The hardened images intended for runtime don't contain a shell nor any tools for debugging.

These are some of the key differences:

Feature Docker Official Node.js Docker Hardened Node.js
Shell access Full shell (bash/sh) available No shell in runtime variants
Package manager npm/yarn available in all variants npm/yarn only available in dev variants

The docs also suggest some options for debugging:

Common debugging methods for applications built with Docker Hardened Images include:

  • Docker Debug to attach to containers
  • Docker's Image Mount feature to mount debugging tools
  • Application-level logging and monitoring

Here's an example I put together showing how a multi-stage build can install dependencies with npm and only need Node in the final stage, which can be adapted to use the hardened images like this:

FROM dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23-sfw-dev AS deps

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
# ...add any other files needed for install

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
  npm \
  # ...options
  ci


FROM dhi.io/node:24-alpine3.23

USER node
WORKDIR /app

# get dependencies from deps stage
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules node_modules/

# copy other files, directly or from other stages
# ...

# set file for Node to run
CMD [ "path/to/file.js" ]

Note I'm using Node 24 LTS here; I'd suggest rarely if ever using odd-numbered, non-LTS releases in production. And it was never a good practice to use npm run start in the container.
